Israel: President Herzog gives the mandate to Eisenkot, not Netanyahu, but the path to a coalition remains narrow

President Isaac Herzog has picked Gadi Eisenkot, a former chief of staff and leader of the Yashar party, rather than Benjamin Netanyahu to try to form the next government. The mandate is due to be handed over officially on Sunday, November 8, at 5 p.m.; Eisenkot will have 28 days, but the arithmetic is difficult [1][2][4].

Herzog announced on November 7 that he was giving the first chance to form a coalition to Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's opponent, after the October 27 election that gave neither camp a majority; the mandate is due to be handed over officially on Sunday at 5 p.m. [1][2][3].

About 67 lawmakers recommended Eisenkot to Herzog, including members of Arab-led parties, against 46 for Netanyahu [1][2]. On the Jewish-led side of the opposition, i24NEWS counts Yashar (21 seats), Naftali Bennett's Beyahad (12), Yair Golan's The Democrats (8) and Avigdor Lieberman's Yisrael Beiteinu (7) [5].

The final results give 53 seats to Netanyahu's bloc, 48 to the opposition and 19 to the Arab parties, out of 120: 61 votes are needed to govern [6]. Likud remains the largest party with 27 seats, six more than Yashar [2].

Eisenkot is calling for a "national emergency government" [7] and may have to settle for a minority government, according to CNN [1]; i24NEWS reports that he is looking at a scenario in which Ra'am and United Torah Judaism would abstain instead of voting against [8].

The obstacles are many: most Jewish-led opposition parties had sworn before the vote not to depend on the votes of Arab parties, Avigdor Lieberman has become a stubborn obstacle, and the ultra-Orthodox Shas party called reports that it would join Eisenkot "complete fake news" [1].
If Eisenkot fails within his 28 days, extendable by 14, Herzog can give the task to another lawmaker; in the meantime, Netanyahu stays on as caretaker prime minister [1][5].

Key point: Netanyahu no longer controls the first step. Herzog was not obliged to choose the leader of the largest party or the one with the most recommendations [5], and he ruled in favor of the challenger.

But a mandate is not a victory. The 67 votes behind Eisenkot come from a camp stretching from Yisrael Beiteinu to the Arab parties, and it is precisely their union that is stuck: the Jewish-led opposition parties do not want to govern with the support of Arab parties, whose votes are nonetheless needed to reach 61 [1].

During these 28 days, Netanyahu keeps power on a caretaker basis [1]: the country's major decisions, on the war as well as on regional negotiations, therefore remain in the hands of an outgoing government. The longer forming a government takes, the longer political uncertainty lasts, which matters for the region and for energy markets.

If Israel stays without a stable coalition for several weeks, it is one more source of uncertainty for the Middle East, and therefore for the price of the oil and diesel you pay for. What to watch: the handover of the mandate on Sunday, then the 28 days.

Hormuz: new "minor" strikes on Iran, but Qatar denies talks have failed and Rubio says nothing is decided

Donald Trump speaks of "minor" strikes on an Iranian air-defense system near Qeshm Island, while Marco Rubio says no decision has been made on further attacks. Qatar, which is pushing a plan to reopen Hormuz within two days, denies that the talks have failed [1][2][3][4].

Donald Trump confirmed new "limited" US strikes on an Iranian air-defense system near Qeshm Island, in the Strait of Hormuz, which he calls "minor" [1][2]. Iranian media report two missiles hitting the island, with no official damage assessment [1].
On Saturday, November 7, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the president had not made a decision on further strikes, as peace talks are stalled [3][4].

Qatar proposes reopening the strait within two days: the United States would lift its blockade and Iran would let nuclear inspectors in. Neither Washington nor Tehran has explicitly rejected the plan [4].
Qatar's International Media Office calls social media posts claiming its prime minister said the talks had failed "false and misleading" [4].
A senior Iranian official says he passed a nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar on Thursday, while making further talks conditional on sanctions relief and an end to the US blockade [4].
In the strait, another tanker reports an explosion near its waterline; the crew is safe [4]. A prominent Iranian lawmaker threatens retaliation if the United States or Israel launch new attacks [4].
Trump says Iranian representatives want a deal and that negotiations are moving forward [4]; earlier in November, Tehran called the US reply to the Hormuz plan "unconvincing" [5].

Key point: Washington is striking in a limited way while saying negotiations are advancing, and each side sets its conditions before moving: lifting the blockade on one side, nuclear inspections on the other. Qatar acts as the go-between [4].

The economic stake is the Strait of Hormuz: as long as it stays blocked or threatened, Gulf oil and gas flow poorly and energy prices stay high. The Qatari plan trades the two key demands, which makes it the most concrete way on the table to reopen the route [4].
A single incident, such as a tanker hit or one strike too many, can derail the two-day timetable. That is what makes the oil market very sensitive to every announcement from either side.
If Hormuz reopens, oil and diesel could fall; if strikes resume on a large scale, the opposite. Pump prices therefore follow these announcements with a lag of a few days.

China keeps its diesel at home: exports expected to plunge in November as stocks hit their lowest in almost seven years

Chinese diesel exports could fall to about 800,000 tonnes in November, against 1.8 million in September, because the country's stocks are at their lowest in almost seven years. Beijing has nevertheless widened its fourth-quarter export quota, but a quota is not a cargo [1][2][4].

According to estimates based on Reuters and traders, China could export about 800,000 tonnes of diesel in November, against 1.33 million in August and 1.8 million in September; refiners have sold only about 500,000 tonnes for November loading [2].

Consultancy Energy Aspects cut its November forecast by 400,000 tonnes, to 580,000 tonnes, because of very low domestic stocks, and says Beijing could ease its brakes if domestic demand weakens [1][3].

Commercial refined-product stocks are at their lowest in almost seven years, according to GL Consulting, Mysteel's think tank, which nonetheless does not expect a nationwide suspension of diesel exports in November [4].
Beijing has widened the fourth-quarter refined-product export quota to 20.44 million tonnes, 44% more than a year earlier, but this extra quota does not guarantee more cargoes [2].

Policy has shifted from month to month since the Middle East crisis: restrictions on fuel exports between April and July [2], then a suspension in October of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel exports to rebuild stocks, according to Reuters [5][6].
According to Kpler, cited in that Reuters report, commercial gasoil and diesel stocks remained about 20 million barrels below their pre-war level [5].
As early as September, Energy Aspects judged that Beijing could cap its fourth-quarter exports of clean products at about 1.2 million tonnes a month [7].

Key point: China, the world's top oil importer, is also a key fuel supplier to Asia. According to the International Energy Agency, its refined-product exports were an essential source of supply for Asian markets in the third quarter; when it keeps its diesel, buyers have to source elsewhere [8].

Diesel powers trucks, tractors, ships and much of industry: when it is scarce, transport costs more. With Middle East exports disrupted by the war, diesel markets are under extreme pressure, says the IEA, and China is adjusting its sales abroad to protect its own market first [8].
A quota is only a permit: it is stocks and government choices that decide cargoes. That is why analysts follow licenses and actual loadings month after month rather than the quota itself [2][4].

Chinese diesel does not end up at French pumps, but it weighs on the global diesel market: less Chinese diesel means more competition among buyers. It is one factor that can keep diesel from falling, even when crude oil retreats.

Ghana: the IMF endorses the first review of its no-loan program, but worries about falling foreign-exchange reserves

The IMF and Ghana reached a staff-level agreement on November 5 on the first review of the country's 36-month monitoring program, which brings no fresh money. Growth of 5.7% is expected in 2026 and inflation was 5.5% in October, but declining foreign-exchange reserves are a concern [1][2][5].

An IMF mission worked in Accra from October 22 to November 4, 2026; the staff-level agreement, announced on November 5, covers the first review of the Policy Coordination Instrument (PCI), a 36-month program [1][3].
The agreement still has to be approved by IMF management and its Executive Board, which is due to discuss the review by January 15, 2027 [1].
A PCI carries no financing: it provides no new loan, but sets a reform course that the IMF assesses regularly [5].

Real GDP grew 6.2% year on year in the first half of 2026, and the IMF expects 5.7% for the full year [2]. Inflation was 5.5% in October, below the Bank of Ghana's target band (8% plus or minus 2 points) [1].

The weak point is foreign-exchange reserves, which have fallen in recent months: the IMF asks for them to be rebuilt, through reform of the Bank of Ghana's liquidity management and a more flexible exchange rate [1][5].

Eight priorities are listed, including rolling out the integrated tax administration system, setting up the Fiscal Council and preparing a fiscal risk statement; Ghana also completed ahead of schedule a review of its customs and excise legislation [4].
The IMF cites among the risks gold, cocoa and oil prices, geopolitical tensions and tighter global financial conditions [3].

Key point: Ghana is no longer in an emergency, but it remains under watch. Its previous $3 billion lending program passed its first review in October 2023 [6]; this time the Fund provides no fresh money, it judges progress [5].

Foreign-exchange reserves are the dollars the central bank keeps to pay for imports and defend the currency. If they fall too far, the cedi becomes more fragile and import prices rise. Gold and cocoa are among the risks cited by the IMF: their prices influence the inflow of foreign currency, and therefore reserves [3].

A more flexible exchange rate means the currency can move more against the dollar instead of being held artificially; it is unpopular in the short term, but the IMF considers it necessary to rebuild reserves [1][5].

This IMF monitoring without a loan shows a country that has regained some room for maneuver, but whose strength still depends on gold and cocoa prices [3]. Worth watching if you follow emerging markets.

Kazakhstan: oil giant Tengiz loses 12.7% of its output, strangled by drone attacks on its export route

Kazakhstan's Tengiz field produced 26.6 million tonnes of oil in nine months, 12.7% less than a year earlier, after drone attacks disrupted the CPC terminal on the Black Sea. Astana now targets 96 million tonnes for 2026 [1][2][5].

According to Reuters, relayed by The Moscow Times on November 3, Tengiz output fell 12.7% over the first nine months of 2026, to 26.6 million tonnes; Tengizchevroil confirms 26.6 million tonnes, about 212.3 million barrels [1][2].

The weak point is the CPC, the pipeline and Black Sea terminal through which about 80% of Kazakhstan's exported oil passes [5]. In July, drone attacks, suspected to be Ukrainian, forced the CPC to suspend loadings [4].

After that halt, Tengiz output fell to about 406,000 barrels a day, against an average of 925,000 in July, according to sources cited by Reuters [4]; national output dropped 21%, according to the Times of Central Asia [3].
Kazakhstan has lowered its 2026 target to 96 million tonnes of oil and gas condensate, against 98 million and then 100.5 million planned earlier [5]; the 2027 target is about 99 million [6].
Tengizchevroil is owned 50% by Chevron, 25% by ExxonMobil, 20% by KazMunayGas and 5% by Lukoil [3].
Meanwhile, Astana plans to commission about 200 industrial enterprises by the end of 2026, for about 1.7 trillion tenge ($3.76 billion), according to Xinhua [6].

Key point: Kazakhstan does not lack oil, it lacks routes to export it. A huge share of its exports goes through a single terminal on the Black Sea, which the war in Ukraine puts directly at risk [5][4].

When Tengiz output falls, there is less crude on a market already tense because of the Gulf war. Europe has already felt it: Euronews reported in February that the continent had lost Kazakh oil after attacks in the Black Sea [7].

For listed groups, it is a direct loss of earnings: Chevron and ExxonMobil together own three quarters of Tengizchevroil [3]. For the Kazakh state, it is a hole in revenue that contrasts with its industrial investment plan [6].

When a major producer like Kazakhstan cannot export, there is a bit less oil on the world market, so a risk of higher prices for the diesel you pay for. It is not the main cause, Iran weighs more, but it is one more factor.

France: the government wants the minimum wage above 1,500 euros net, ahead of Monday's social conference

On the eve of the social conference at Matignon, Labour Minister Jean-Pierre Farandou says he wants to cross the "1,500 euros net bar": the net minimum wage (Smic) is currently 1,477.93 euros. A decree is "ready" to push industry sectors to raise their minimum pay scales, and the unions are asking for far more [1][2][3].

On Monday, November 9, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu brings unions and employers together at Matignon for a "social conference" on purchasing power and wages, four days after the national strike of November 5 [1][4].
The Interior Ministry counted 575,000 demonstrators on November 5; the unions claim about 1.5 million, a gap seen after every big day of action [3].

On Friday, November 6, Jean-Pierre Farandou said it was "important" to try to cross the 1,500 euros net bar, while the net Smic is 1,477.93 euros: about 22 euros a month would be missing, an increase of roughly 1.5% (our calculation from these two figures) [2][3].
He added that a decree was "ready": it would aim to push industry sectors to raise their minimum pay scales, failing which the payroll-tax relief tied to those wages would be affected [2][3].
The minister said talks would continue until Sunday to seek a compromise between the social partners on the Smic, sector minimums and wage negotiations [2].

On the unions' side, according to AFP quoted by Qz, the CFDT asks for 100 euros more net per month, the CGT for a 10% rise and Force Ouvrière for a 2,000-euro Smic; the CGT also wants all wages indexed to prices [1].
The unions' joint committee is to decide on the next steps of the mobilization after Monday's meeting [1].

Key point: the Smic is the only wage the state sets itself, so it is the first lever the government can pull quickly. Going from 1,477.93 to more than 1,500 euros net would be a modest gesture in value, far from what the unions ask: 100 euros for the CFDT, 10% for the CGT, 2,000 euros for FO [1][2].

The decree on sectors shows the real sticking point. Each industry sector sets its own minimum pay scales: when the Smic rises, those that stay too low have to follow. According to the minister, the decree aims to push sectors to raise their minimums, failing which the payroll-tax relief tied to those wages would be affected, which puts part of the effort on companies [2][3].

For the government the equation is tight: a wage rise costs employers and, through payroll-tax relief, the state budget, just as the 2027 budget bill has been rejected by the National Assembly. That is why Matignon talks of a "compromise" between the social partners rather than a unilateral decision [1][2].

The mobilization, for its part, remains strong: the unions come to the table with the argument of a large-scale strike and repeated Saturday demonstrations. What comes out on Monday will show whether the movement calms down or continues [1][3][4].

If you earn the minimum wage, a rise of about 22 euros net per month would take your pay above 1,500 euros; if your sector has low minimums, the decree could improve your pay scale. If you are an employer, it is your labour cost that is being discussed. Either way, Monday's announcements are what will count, not the figures mentioned before the meeting.

2027 budget: the Assembly rejected everything, 458 votes to zero, and the per-gigabyte tax disappears with the rest

On Wednesday, November 4, MPs rejected the revenue part of the 2027 state budget by 458 votes to none, with two abstentions according to France 24. The text goes to the Senate in its original version, and the government keeps the 49.3 procedure or ordinances in reserve [1][2][3].

On November 4, 2026, the National Assembly rejected the first part of the finance bill, the revenue part, by 458 votes against, none in favor and two abstentions, according to France 24 and franceinfo [1][2].
This rejection stops the examination: with the revenue part not adopted, MPs cannot move on to spending, and the government's original text is sent to the Senate [1][2].

During three weeks of debate, MPs had heavily amended the bill: the surtax on big companies, meant to raise 5 billion euros in 2027, had notably been removed. All those amendments fall with the rejection [1][3].

Among them, the per-gigabyte tax: an amendment by Socialist MP Laurent Lhardit, adopted on Friday, October 30 by 11 votes to 10, with only 35 of 577 MPs present, created a tax payable by content providers. Clubic and Yahoo cite 5.5 cents per gigabyte; Next speaks of 10 cents for the PS's initial plan [4][5].
The tax's supporters hoped for 10 billion euros a year, a figure the government disputed; no rise in internet subscriptions had been decided [4][5].

According to 20 Minutes, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu had a non-censure agreement with the Socialist Party, but no compromise is in sight at this stage; the effort asked of the country is about 54 billion euros to bring the deficit to 5% of GDP in 2027 [3][6].

According to franceinfo, the Senate would examine the text from November 20; NosParlementaires mentions a schedule for the revenue part running until November 28 or 29, subject to confirmation [2][6].

Key point: a unanimous rejection does not mean everyone refuses the same thing. The 458 votes come from all groups, including those that support the government, according to 20 Minutes: the text no longer had a majority, whatever each group's reasons [3].

The figure that matters is the effort, about 54 billion euros, to return to a deficit of 5% of GDP in 2027. Without a voted budget, the government must choose between finding a majority in the Senate and then the Assembly, using the 49.3 at the risk of a no-confidence motion, or going through a budget ordinance, an option mentioned by France 24 [1][3][6].

The per-gigabyte tax episode shows another risk: a measure voted in an almost empty chamber, 11 votes to 10, caused an uproar before being erased five days later with the rejection of the budget; its possible bill for households had not been settled [4][5].

For now, nothing changes in your daily life: no tax is in force and last year's rules continue to apply. But the outcome of the budget will decide taxes, benefits and public spending for 2027. Remember the date to watch: the Senate, from late November, then the search for a compromise in December.

Spain: Renfe train drivers strike on Tuesday and Thursday, less than two weeks after the Urda rail disaster

The drivers' union Semaf is maintaining a full strike on Tuesday, November 10 and partial stoppages on Thursday the 12th, despite the resignation of Transport Minister Óscar Puente after the Urda crash (69 dead). The government has set minimum services of 72% on high-speed lines [1][2][3].

On October 28, 2026, at about 8:54 a.m., a Renfe AVE train hit the back of a stationary Iryo train near Urda (Toledo province) on the Madrid-Seville line: 69 dead, after a computer failure of the LZB automatic signalling system, according to Al Jazeera and Yahoo [1][4].

Transport Minister Óscar Puente resigned on November 3, judging that a transport minister could not stay in office after two serious accidents in less than a year; the next day the president of the track manager Adif, Luis Pedro Marco de la Peña, left his post [4][5].

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez temporarily gave the ministry to his first deputy prime minister and Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo. Óscar Puente also withdrew from the lists for the early election of November 29 [4][5].

Semaf maintains a full strike on Tuesday, November 10 and partial stoppages on Thursday, November 12; according to the union quoted by the local press, it demands "real commitments" on safety and was not satisfied with the minister's departure [2][6].

The Transport Ministry set minimum services: 72% on high-speed and long-distance, 65% on medium-distance, 75% at rush hour and 50% for the rest of the day on commuter trains (Cercanías), and 20% for freight [2][3].
Urda is the second fatal accident on this corridor in nine months: a derailment near Adamuz (Córdoba) had killed 46 people in January [4].
Key point: the strike is not a pay dispute but a safety one. The drivers want guarantees after two disasters, and the minister's resignation is not enough to reassure them [2][6].

Traffic will not come to a halt: with 72% minimum services, most high-speed trains should run on Tuesday, but commuter trips and freight will be hit harder. For freight, only 20% of planned services are guaranteed, which can delay deliveries [2][3].

The political context weighs: Spain votes on November 29, and the opposition Popular Party welcomed the minister's departure without judging it sufficient as political responsibility [4][5]. On the investigation side, specialists are examining the failure of the LZB system and the instructions then given by Adif's control centre at Madrid-Atocha [4].

If you travel in Spain on Tuesday, November 10 or Thursday, November 12, check your train on Renfe: high-speed is kept at 72%, but commuter and medium-distance timetables will be reduced. On the economic side, only 20% of freight services are guaranteed, which can delay deliveries.

EU: finance ministers meet in Brussels on Monday, with a tobacco tax and the digital euro on the agenda

On Monday, November 9, the Eurogroup and then the Ecofin Council meet in Brussels, ahead of a budget Ecofin on the 10th. On the agenda: a political agreement on tobacco taxation, an update on the digital euro, decisions under the stability pact and the economic effect of the war in Ukraine [1][2].

On Monday, November 9, 2026, euro-area finance ministers meet in the Eurogroup, then those of the EU in the Ecofin Council; an Ecofin on the budget follows on November 10, according to the official calendar of the EU Council [1][2].

The Eurogroup is to review the economic and budgetary situation of the euro area after the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok in October, with inflation and national budget discussions on the agenda [1].

The European Central Bank will present the state of negotiations and its technical preparations on the digital euro, as well as on wholesale central bank payments; the chairs of the ECB supervisory board and the Single Resolution Board will update ministers on the banking sector [1].

The Ecofin is invited to reach a political agreement on the "tobacco package": raising minimum excise duties in the EU and extending the rules to new products (e-cigarettes, heated tobacco, nicotine pouches), on the Commission's proposal of July 2025 [1][3].

According to a Vital Signs preview, disagreements persist over nicotine pouches, traditional products and minimum rates, although a senior EU official is cautiously optimistic; Council working documents show that the rate on pouches has varied from one draft to another [3][4].
Ministers must also take decisions under the stability and growth pact, discuss simplification of EU legislation, and assess the economic and financial impact of Russia's war against Ukraine [1].
An AFP dispatch carried by TradingView mentions the examination of candidacies for the ECB presidency, which the official agenda does not mention: this remains to be confirmed [5].

Key point: these meetings do not make the front page, but they settle concrete things, such as the price of tobacco across the EU or the timetable of the digital euro. A "political agreement" is an agreement in principle between ministers on a text [1][3].

The tobacco tax is a test for states: raising the minimums could force some countries to increase their excise duties, and nicotine pouches, a recent market, divide countries over their level of taxation [3][4].

The digital euro is another issue: the idea is an electronic version of central bank money, usable by everyone. On Monday the ECB presents the state of negotiations and its technical preparations: the project is therefore still under discussion [1].
Finally, the stability pact frames each country's debt and deficit: the decisions planned for Monday come while several states, including France, are still negotiating their budgets [1].

If you smoke or vape, a European agreement on tobacco and nicotine could eventually push up prices in your country, but not before formal adoption and entry into force. As for the digital euro, nothing changes today: it does not exist yet and the timetable depends on texts the EU still has to vote.

Serbia: the failure of Alta Banka, a bank widely used by Russians living in Belgrade, shakes the region

Serbia's central bank withdrew Alta Banka's licence on October 30, and a Belgrade court opened bankruptcy proceedings on November 3. Deposits are guaranteed up to 50,000 euros; beyond that, customers, many of them Russians, have lost access to their savings [1][2][3].

On October 30, 2026, the National Bank of Serbia withdrew Alta Banka's licence after a sharp deterioration in its financial position; sources differ by a day (October 30 or 31) on the exact date [3][4][5].

The Belgrade commercial court opened bankruptcy proceedings on November 3 and named the Deposit Insurance Agency as administrator; the state-owned bank Banka Poštanska štedionica handles the payouts [3][4].
The guarantee is 50,000 euros per depositor; the agency has seven working days to pay out, and balances above the cap are filed as claims in the bankruptcy [3][4].
Queues formed outside branches on October 31, but the Association of Serbian Banks said it was an isolated case with no effect on other banks [3][4].
Alta Banka held about 3% of the Serbian market and served the Russian community living in Serbia heavily; BIRN met customers who lost access to funds meant to buy a home in the country [1][5].
The anti-corruption prosecutor had three officials arrested; the bank's owner, Davor Macura, is suspected by the authorities of embezzling more than 427 million dollars, according to the press [5].
Several media describe the bank as close to the outgoing government, after Aleksandar Vučić's defeat in the parliamentary election: this is a journalistic assessment, not an established fact [2][5].

Key point: a bank failure is first of all a matter of trust. A depositor in a struggling bank may lose access to accounts for a few days, but the 50,000-euro guarantee protects the vast majority of savers. Large accounts, those of companies or wealthy people, are most at risk [3][4].

This episode affects a specific population: the Russian community living in Serbia, very present among the bank's customers. Many lost access to their savings beyond the guarantee cap, which shows the risk of concentrating funds in a single bank [1][5].

For the Serbian banking sector, the authorities' message is soundness: the Association of Banks and the specialist press speak of an individual case. The question is now political and judicial: the investigation will say whether funds were really embezzled abroad and who benefited [3][4][5].

This story is a reminder of a simple reflex: in France as in Serbia, deposit insurance protects a limited sum per bank, and anything above is not insured. Nothing changes for your bank, but it is the reason large amounts are sometimes spread out.

Intesa-MPS: the giant bank offer rises to €31.4 billion, and Siena's shareholders rejected their own management's counterattack

Intesa Sanpaolo has raised its exchange offer for Monte dei Paschi (MPS) to €31.4 billion: 1.664 Intesa shares and €1.25 in cash for each MPS share. A few days earlier, MPS shareholders had rejected, by more than 90%, their own management's offers for Banco BPM and Banca Generali [2][3][4].

How it works: an exchange offer

A public tender and exchange offer (OPAS) invites the target's shareholders to sell their shares in return for a mix of the buyer's shares and cash. Here: 1.664 Intesa shares plus €1.25 for one MPS share. Because the share part follows Intesa's price, the value offered rises and falls every day, so the buyer adjusts the ratio from time to time. The target can defend itself by refusing, by looking for another buyer, or by launching its own offer for other companies to become bigger and harder to swallow. Shareholders decide by tendering or not, and the authorities check competition (antitrust) and national security (golden power) [3][4].

How it works: a non-binding offer, premium and milestone payments

A non-binding offer is a proposal that commits neither the buyer nor the target: the target's board can refuse it, negotiate, or look for other buyers. When the news breaks, the target's share price rises toward the proposed price but stays below it: the gap reflects the risk that the deal will not happen. The price can include milestone payments: part is paid only if the drug reaches targets set in advance, such as an approval or a sales level. The buyer thus pays less up front, and the target shares the risk [1].

How it works: why gold falls when rates rise

Gold pays neither interest nor dividends. A bond or an account pays a rate. When rates rise, what you give up by holding gold, the interest you could have earned, grows: this is called opportunity cost, and some buyers turn to bonds. The dollar matters too: gold is priced in dollars, so the dearer the dollar, the dearer the ounce in other currencies, which holds back demand. Conversely, gold rises when rates fall or when people fear a crisis [1][2].
